title: Hávamál
source: Gustav Neckel, Edda: Die Lieder des Codex Regius nebst verwandten Denkmälern, 1st edition (Heidelberg: Carl Winter, 1914), Hávamál, stanzas 111–137, pp. 33–38. Text transcribed from Neckel's page images and reproduced in his normalization exactly — þ, ð, æ, œ, the nasal vowel ǫ, ø, acute length-marks, the -z/-az/-oz middle endings and the -mk middles, i for j (sitia, nióta, fiǫlkunnigri), -om datives, þvíat as one word. Italicized (editorially emended or expanded) letters are set as plain letters; the emendations that change the sense are noted. Neckel's square brackets marking 121,8–10 as an interpolation and his asterisk at 137,11 (*hǫll) marking a corrupt half-line are kept. In his apparatus, bold sigla are manuscripts (R = Codex Regius, F = Flateyiarbók, H = Hauksbók) and italic sigla are scholars (Mh = Müllenhoff, R = Rask, D = Dietrich, J = Finnur Jónsson, Hs = Heusler, Gv = Grundtvig, B = Bugge, G = Gering, H = Hildebrand, Mk = Mogk, S = Sijmons, W = Wimmer); the notes here follow that distinction, and say so at the two places in this part where the collision decides the reading — 111,4, where the italic R is Rask and not the Codex Regius, and 135,6, where the italic H is Hildebrand and not the Hauksbók. Eddic poems are cited by stanza, so the margin numbers are stanza numbers. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed classical Old Icelandic, c. 1200 — and the recorded reading follows it, within one honest limit. No Icelandic synthetic voice exists that accepts phonetic instruction, so the reading is produced by a German neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to a modern language's habits. This deliberately avoids the eight centuries of change that separate modern Icelandic from the poem — hv is [hw], as in English 'what', not the modern [kv]; ǫ is [ɔ], not ö; á and ó are pure vowels, not diphthongs; ll is a plain lateral, not the modern [tl]; and final -r, the nominative ending on hundreds of these words, is voiced rather than whispered. The limit: the carrier admits only two long vowels, so Old Norse's long/short contrast is carried by vowel quality (á/a, é/e, í/i, ó/o, ú/u, ý/y all stay distinct) rather than by true duration, and long consonants are read short. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: The Loddfáfnismál — the counsels given to Loddfáfnir, which Neckel prints as a separate movement after the rule at stanza 110 and which the paper manuscripts head with that name. A speaker announces that it is time to chant from the sage's seat at Urðr's well, says he stood at the High One's hall and listened, and then delivers what he heard: some two dozen pieces of counsel, nearly every one of them introduced by the same four-line refrain — I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel. The advice is practical and unsentimental. Do not rise at night unless you are standing watch or going out to relieve yourself. Do not sleep in the arms of a woman skilled in magic. Visit a friend often, because the road no one treads grows over with brushwood. Do not be a shoemaker unless you are making the shoe for yourself. Do not laugh at an old reciter: what comes out of a shrivelled bag is often sound. It closes with a catalogue of remedies — earth against ale, fire against sickness, oak against constipation — in which the last items are half-broken and the editor marks one half-line as corrupt. Who Loddfáfnir is nobody knows; the name occurs only here. Heusler thought stanza 111 belonged instead to the runic poem that follows at 138. Everything printed here is a modern editor's normalization of a single manuscript, the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270); the verse is ljóðaháttr, and the margin numbers are stanza numbers.

sentences.t:
Mál er at þylia
þular stóli á,
Urðar brunni at;
sá ek ok þagðak,
sá ek ok hugðak,
hlýdda ek á manna mál:
of rúnar heyrða ek dœma,
né um ráðom þǫgðo,
Háva hǫllo at,
Háva hǫllo í,
heyrða ek segia svá:
sentences.l:
It is time to chant
on the sage's seat,
at Urðr's well;
I saw and I was silent,
I saw and I pondered,
I listened to the speech of men:
of runes I heard men discourse,
nor about counsels were they silent,
at the High One's hall,
in the High One's hall,
I heard men say thus:
sentences.i: Now is the time to speak from the sage's seat, at Urðr's well. I watched and said nothing; I watched and thought; I listened to what men were saying. I heard them discourse of runes, and they were not silent about counsel either — at the High One's hall, inside the High One's hall, this is what I heard said:
sentences.n: Neckel prints a rule before this stanza, and the paper manuscripts head 111–137 Loddfáfnismál; the Codex Regius itself marks a break here too — Neckel notes that its M in Mál 111,1 is very large and set out into the margin. His apparatus adds that Heusler took 111 instead as the introduction to the Rúnatal of 138 ff. The stanza reads like the opening of something, and no one is certain of what. A þulr is a reciter of ancient lore — the word behind fimbulþulr in st. 80 — and his stóll is the seat he speaks from; þylia is what he does on it, chant or mutter the traditional matter over. Urðr's well is the spring of fate under the world-tree, so the seat stands where what is fixed is known. Two of the four verbs of hearing and speaking have no expressed subject: of rúnar heyrða ek dœma and heyrða ek segia svá are accusative-and-infinitive with the accusative withheld, and the 'men' supplied in both lines here is taken from manna mál in line 6, which is also the unexpressed subject of þǫgðo. The apparatus is unusually full. In line 2 the manuscript has á with a point after it and at added above by a later hand; in line 3 its vrþar is indistinct and the same later hand repeated vrðar in the margin. In line 4 Rask conjectured sat ek, 'I sat', for the manuscript's sá ek, 'I saw' — a reading Resen's edition already had — and against line 5 Neckel sets the bare query sat ek?, asking whether the same change belongs there. Neckel keeps the manuscript's sá ek in both lines. So the manuscript is clear; it is the editors who cannot decide whether the sage sits and keeps silence or watches and keeps silence. In line 6 Müllenhoff conjectured Háva for the manuscript's manna, comparing the poem's closing stanza 164, and deleted lines 7–11 altogether. Eleven lines.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
at þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
nótt þú rísat,
nema á niósn séir
eða þú leitir þér innan út staðar.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
that you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
by night rise you not,
unless you be on the watch
or you seek yourself a place out from within.
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and you should take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: do not get up at night, unless you are standing watch, or unless you are going outside to relieve yourself.
sentences.n: The frame, glossed here once and taken as read afterwards: nearly every stanza from here to 137 opens with these same four lines. Ráðomk is ráða with the -mk middle ending, 'I counsel', the speaker folded into the verb — the ending of létomk and stóðomk in st. 106. nema is both 'to take' and 'to learn', so ráð nema is at once accepting advice and getting it by heart; nem in st. 120 is the same verb. mundo is munt þú, 'you will', with the pronoun fused on, and góð is neuter plural agreeing with the unspoken ráð. The two conditions in lines 3–4 differ only in the verb, nemr 'take' and getr 'get'. Neckel prints at þú ráð nemir here and in 113 and 115, which is the manuscript's reading, and en from 116 on; Rask wanted en here too, comparing Fáfnismál 20,2, where the dying Fáfnir gives Sigurðr the same second line — 'Ræð ek þér nú, Sigurðr — en þú ráð nemir' — so the half-line is a formula of counsel outside this poem as well. From 113 on the scribe stops writing the frame out and abbreviates it to initials (see the note to 116) — the manuscript treats it as a refrain, which is a fair guide to how it should be read. The counsel proper starts at line 5, and it is a prohibition, not a prediction: rísat is the imperative rís with the suffixed negative -at, 'rise not' — the 2 sg. present indicative would be ríss — the same shape as Haldit maðr á keri in st. 19, and distinct from the skalattu of 113 and the þú skalt aldregi of 122, which do use skulu. Neckel's þú rísat is corrected from the manuscript's þún sat, which he calls a misreading; his séir has an editorial i, the manuscript reading sér. leita sér staðar, 'to seek oneself a place', is the ordinary euphemism for stepping outside to relieve oneself, and innan út is 'out from indoors'.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
at þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
fiǫlkunnigri kono
skalattu í faðmi sofa,
svá at hon lyki þik liðom.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
that you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
with a magic-wise woman
you shall not sleep in embrace,
so that she shut you in with her limbs.
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and you should take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: never sleep in the arms of a woman skilled in magic — she will shut you in fast with her own limbs.
sentences.n: skalattu packs three things into one word: skalt, the suffixed negative -a, and the enclitic pronoun þú. fiǫlkunnigr is 'much-knowing', and the knowledge meant is witchcraft. lyki is the weak verb lykia, 'to shut in, enclose', not lúka 'to close, finish' — lúka is strong and its subjunctive would be lúki, with a long vowel. lykia takes the accusative, so þik is its object and liðom is an instrumental dative: she shuts you in with her limbs, and the word for limbs is the word for joints. The danger is not stated here; the next stanza is the consequence clause. The apparatus records that the manuscript's skaltu was corrected to skalatu, with a firra þik after it cancelled by underdots.

sentences.t:
Hón svá gørir,
at þú gáir eigi
þings né þióðans máls;
mat þú villat
né mannzkis gaman,
ferr þú sorgafullr at sofa.
sentences.l:
She so works it,
that you heed not
the assembly nor a lord's speech;
food you want not
nor any man's delight,
you go sorrow-full to sleep.
sentences.i: She will bring it about that you take no notice of the assembly or of a lord's word; you will want no food and no delight in anyone, and you will go to your bed full of grief.
sentences.n: No frame, because this is not a new counsel: 114 is the second half of 113, the consequence of sleeping in those arms. gá governs the genitive, hence þings and máls; Fritzner would read line 3's þióðans máls as one word, þióðarmáls — which also means altering the genitive, þióðar for þióðans, so that the phrase would be something like 'public speech' rather than 'a lord's word'. Neckel records the conjecture and keeps the manuscript's two words. villat is vill with the suffixed negative -at, and the subject is still þú: Neckel's vill- is the older 2nd singular of vilia, where the usual form is vilt (ef þú vilt, st. 98). mannzkis is the genitive of manngi, 'no one', which in a negative clause comes out as 'anyone'. Notice what the spell is said to cost — exactly the public world the Gestaþáttr spent seventy stanzas teaching a man to move in: the assembly, the lord's word, food, company, and sleep. né mannzkis gaman is st. 47 turned inside out — maðr er mannz gaman, 'man is man's delight', was the Gestaþáttr's plainest statement of what makes life worth living, and the spell takes exactly that away.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
at þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
annars kono
teygðo þér aldregi
eyrarúno at.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
that you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
another's wife
entice to yourself never
as an ear-confidante.
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and you should take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: never entice another man's wife into being your own intimate.
sentences.n: eyrarúna is an 'ear-rune' — the person you whisper to — and rún here carries the older sense, a secret or whispered counsel, that stands behind the letters. The lexica use the word of a wife or a beloved as well as of a confidante, so the counsel is not against sharing secrets but against taking another man's wife as your own intimate; the word keeps the whispering in it, which is how the euphemism works. at is postposed and governs the dative eyrarúno. teygia is the verb of st. 102, where Óðinn drew the wise woman into a trick; it returns in st. 120 with the opposite instruction, which is how this run of counsels works — the same act forbidden with one person and commanded with another.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
á fialli eða firði
ef þik fara tíðir,
fástu at virði vel.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and do you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
on fell or on firth,
if it take you to travel,
get yourself well provided with food.
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: if you have a mind to travel, over the fell or along the fjord, see that you are well provisioned.
sentences.n: From here on Neckel prints en þú ráð nemir where 112–115 had at, and it makes line 2 a second exhortation rather than a clause depending on the first. What the manuscript gives is less clean than that sounds. Only at 112 does the scribe write the frame out, and there it reads at; from 113 he abbreviates it to initials, and Neckel prints the abbreviations he is reading — 113 'Ráðomk þér l. a. þ. r. n. n.'', where the a. is at, and 116 'Ráðomk þér l. f. ē.', where the ē is en. At 115 and 117 the abbreviation stops earlier still ('Ráðomk þ. l.', 'Ráð. þ.') and contains nothing for the word at all, so the reading there is supplied from the pattern. tíða is impersonal and puts the person in the accusative, so ef þik fara tíðir is 'if it takes you to travel'. fástu is the middle fásk with þú fused on, and fásk at is 'to get for oneself'; virði is food, the same word as at virði in st. 32. The plainest counsel in the poem: do not set out hungry.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
illan mann
láttu aldregi
óhǫpp at þér vita;
þvíat af illom manni
fær þú aldregi
giǫld ins góða hugar.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and do you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
an evil man
never let
know of mishaps concerning you;
for from an evil man
you will get never
repayment for the good heart.
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: never let a bad man learn of your misfortunes; for from a bad man you will never get any return for your good heart.
sentences.n: Accusative-and-infinitive with láta, and it repays care which way it runs: illan mann is the accusative subject of vita, so the bad man is the one who would do the knowing, and óhǫpp at þér is what he would know. (The same construction, read backwards, is what turns st. 106 inside out.) The second half is flat arithmetic — giǫld are payments, and there are none to be had from that quarter for ins góða hugar, your good heart. Line 8 comes back verbatim as 123,1, and line 9 is its near-twin: fær þú aldregi here, mundo aldregi there — the same 'never' with munu in place of fá, and the pronoun enclitic instead of free. The counsels are assembled out of reusable blocks, and the scribe's habit of abbreviating shows he read them that way. Ten lines.

sentences.t:
Ofarla bíta
ek sá einom hal
orð illrar kono:
fláráð tunga
varð hánom at fiǫrlagi,
ok þeygi um sanna sǫk.
sentences.l:
High up bite
I saw upon one man
the words of an evil woman:
a false-counselled tongue
became for him a loss of life,
and yet not over a true charge.
sentences.i: I have seen an evil woman's words bite one man high up; a lying tongue was the death of him — and not over anything he had truly done.
sentences.n: A single remembered instance dropped into the counsels, and the only stanza in this run with a witness in it. The syntax is accusative-and-infinitive again, under sá: orð are the biters, and einom hal is dative — halr makes its dative singular hal — so he is the one bitten, not the biter. ofarla is 'high up', and the word alone does not decide whether the wound is high on the body or the bite simply went deep; Neckel's apparatus says nothing here, so the choice is the reader's, and both layers keep the word as it stands. fláráðr is 'false in counsel'; verða e-m at fiǫrlagi is 'to become someone's death'. þeygi is 'and yet not', the negation sitting on the adverb and not on the noun phrase. The sting is the last line: sǫk is a charge at law, so the accusation that killed him was not a true one. Neckel's apparatus notes that a bíta standing after sá in line 2 was cancelled with underdots in the manuscript.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
veitstu, ef þú vin átt,
þannz þú vel trúir,
farðu at finna opt;
þvíat hrísi vex
ok hávo grasi
vegr, er vetki trøðr.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and do you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
know this, if you have a friend,
one whom you trust well,
go to find him often;
for with brushwood grows
and with high grass
the road that nothing treads.
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: you know this — if you have a friend you trust well, go and see him often; for the road nobody walks grows over with brushwood and tall grass.
sentences.n: Lines 5–7 are st. 44 over again, almost word for word — Veitstu, ef þú vin átt, / þann er þú vel trúir, … fara at finna opt — with þannz for þann er and the infinitive turned into the imperative farðu. The Gestaþáttr gave the counsel to a man learning how to live; Loddfáfnismál gives it back as a rule, and adds the image of the untrodden road as its argument. (122's orðom skipta is the same reuse of 44,5 giǫfom skipta.) veitstu is veizt þú, and it can be heard either as a question or as an imperative, 'know this'; the sense comes out the same. The argument is the image in the last three lines: hrísi and grasi are datives of means and vegr is the subject of vex, so the untrodden road grows over of itself. vetki, 'nothing', stands as the subject of trøðr, which English has to turn into 'nobody'. Neckel's apparatus gives vegs, a genitive, as the manuscript's reading against his printed nominative vegr; he cites it against line 8, though the word stands in line 10. Ten lines.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
góðan mann
teygðo þér at gamanrúnom
ok nem líknargaldr, meðan þú lifir.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and do you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
a good man
draw to yourself for glad talk
and learn a healing-charm, while you live.
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: draw a good man to you for cheerful talk, and learn a charm of healing as long as you live.
sentences.n: The mirror of 115. There teygðo was forbidden, with another man's wife, at eyrarúno; here it is commanded, with a good man, at gamanrúnom — 'glad runes', the same rún, whispered talk, in its pleasant sense. líknargaldr is a charm of mercy or healing, and galdr is specifically the chanted spell: this is the first glance forward to the Ljóðatal of 146 ff., where Óðinn counts eighteen of them. nem is the imperative of the verb the frame keeps using for taking counsel, so learning a charm and taking advice are the same word.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
vin þínom
ver þú aldregi
fyrri at flaumslitom.
[sorg etr hiarta,
ef þú segia ne náir
einhveriom allan hug].
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and do you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
to your friend
be you never
the first at a breaking-off.
[Sorrow eats the heart,
if you may not tell
to some one your whole mind.]
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: never be the first to break with a friend. [Sorrow eats the heart if you have no one you can tell your whole mind to.]
sentences.n: flaumslit is a severing — of flaumr, which the lexica give as an eddy, a stream, a rush — though what exactly the first element contributes here is guesswork; the compound is not securely attested outside this line. The counsel is not to be the one who breaks first. vin þínom is dative (vinr makes its dative and accusative singular alike, vin), so the friend is the one you would be breaking with. Lines 8–10 stand in square brackets because Neckel judges them an interpolation; there is no marking in the manuscript, so the brackets are the editor's opinion, and they are kept here rather than removed so that the reader can see the judgment being made instead of having it made silently. They also say in advance what 124 will say at length. ne is the older negative particle, as at st. 93 and 108, and ná is 'to be able, to manage'. Ten lines.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
orðom skipta
þú skalt aldregi
við ósvinna apa;
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and do you take counsel —
profit you will, if you take it,
good for you they will be, if you get them —:
words exchange
you shall never
with an unwise ape;
sentences.i: I have counsel for you, Loddfáfnir, and take it — take it and you will profit by it, get it and it will do you good: never exchange words with an unwise fool —
sentences.n: The stanza does not finish. 123 opens with þvíat and completes the sentence, which is why 123 carries no frame of its own and why the manuscript, which abbreviates the frame for 122, has nothing to abbreviate for 123. skipta takes the dative, so orðom is 'with words' — and orðom skipta answers giǫfom skipta at st. 44,5, exchanging words where friends exchange gifts. api, literally 'ape', is the poem's blunt word for a fool: margr verðr af ǫðrom api at st. 75. ósvinnr is the negative of the sviðr, 'wise', of st. 103.

sentences.t:
þvíat af illom manni
mundo aldregi
góðs laun um geta,
en góðr maðr
mun þik gørva mega
líknfastan at lofi.
sentences.l:
for from an evil man
you will never
get the reward of good,
but a good man
will be able to make you
firm in favour, as to praise.
sentences.i: — for from a bad man you will never get any reward for good, while a good man can make your standing secure in what people say of you.
sentences.n: The completion of 122. Line 1 repeats 117,8 word for word, and line 2 varies 117,9 — mundo aldregi for fær þú aldregi. gørva is the infinitive of gøra, 'to make', not the adverb gǫrva, 'fully', of st. 102 — one letter apart and easy to confuse, so the plain-letters toggle will not help here. líknfastr, 'held fast in favour', is cited by the dictionaries only from this line, and belongs with the líknargaldr of three stanzas back: a small cluster of líkn-, the word for mercy and good will. lof and líkn stood together already at st. 8, of the man who wins for himself lof ok líknstafi, praise and tokens of favour; 123 says the same thing of what a good friend can do for you. at lofi limits it to your standing in what men say.

sentences.i: There is a mingling of kinship when a man undertakes to tell one other person his whole mind. Anything is better than being a breaker of faith; he is no friend to another who says only what is untrue.
sentences.n: The bracketed lines of 121 finished, and the close of the run. blanda takes the dative, and sifiar are the bonds of kin and of marriage, so telling one person your whole mind is described as mixing kinship with him — the same verb as the geði blanda, 'to mingle minds', of st. 44. The comparison in lines 4–5 carries its own finite verb: sé is the 3rd singular present subjunctive of vera heading the clause, with the infinitive phrase as its subject, exactly as at st. 11, en sé manvit mikit. brigð is inconstancy, breach of faith, and vera at brigðom is to be given over to it. The last line is a crux: vilt may be the neuter of villr, 'false', giving 'he who says only what is untrue' — which takes Neckel's vilt as a single-l spelling of villt — or may be connected with vili, 'what pleases', giving 'he who says only what is agreeable', which takes the word as it stands. We translate the first and record the second; the moral survives either way, and the stanza's own contrast carries it — allan hug against vilt eitt, the whole mind against one thing only. Gering proposed the shorter line erat vinr, er vilt eitt segir, dropping sá and ǫðrom and writing erat for the manuscript's era; Neckel records the conjecture without endorsing it, and gives no reason for it.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
þrimr orðom senna
skalattu við þér verra mann;
opt inn betri bilar,
þá er inn verri vegr.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
With three words to wrangle
you shall not with a man worse than yourself;
often the better one fails,
when the worse one fights.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: never trade words — even three of them — with a man worse than yourself; the better man often gives way when the worse one strikes.
sentences.n: The frame, which now runs eleven times to the end of the part, and which the reader should learn to hear as a single breath rather than as four statements. Ráðomk is ráða 'to counsel' with the -mk middle ending, the same formation as létomk and stóðomk at st. 106 and lǫgðomk at st. 108: literally 'I counsel for myself to you', idiomatically just 'I counsel you'. mundo is munt þú with the pronoun fused onto the verb, and nióta governs a genitive whose object is never spoken — the counsels themselves. In the fourth line góð is neuter plural, which is what settles the number: the thing profited by is the counsels, plural, and both layers say 'them'. Here is the general licence, stated once for the whole part: the literal layer supplies in English the words the Norse leaves unsaid — the 'them' of the refrain, the object of láta fast vera at st. 130, the 'your' of á liðo at st. 136 — because English cannot stay silent where Old Norse can. Neckel prints en þú ráð nemir here; up to st. 115 he prints at þú, which his apparatus at 112,2 records as the Codex Regius reading ('at R, en R … ebenso im folg. bis 115'). — Something worth knowing about all four lines: the manuscript does not write them out here. It abbreviates them, and Neckel's apparatus records the abbreviation stanza by stanza — at 125–132, 135 and 137 as '1—4 abgek. wie in 119 R', abgekürzt, 'abbreviated as at 119', and at 134 with the bare 'Ráð. þér'. At st. 119 itself the apparatus gives what the scribe wrote there: 'Ráðomk þér', and then nothing. So the frame is in the manuscript, in shorthand; the refrain as the reader sees it is an editor's expansion of that shorthand, expanded identically every time because that is the editorial convention, not because the scribe wrote it out identically. Loddfáfnir is nobody we can identify: the second element looks like the dragon-name Fáfnir and the first may be loddari 'a vagrant, a jongleur', but the name is attested nowhere else and its meaning is disputed. — In the counsel itself, senna is the technical word for a formal exchange of insults, the flyting; 'three words' is the smallest quantity of it. skalattu is three things at once: skalt, the suffixed negative -at, and the enclitic þú; Neckel's apparatus records that the Codex Regius writes skalatu, corrected by the scribe from skaltu. And við þér verra mann repays slowing down for, because the words do not group the way they look: við governs the accusative mann, while þér is a dative of comparison belonging to the comparative verra — 'with a man worse than you'. The order við þér is Grundtvig's; the manuscript has þér við, which means the same thing. bila is 'to give way, to lose one's nerve', and the point is not that the worse man wins on merit but that the better man declines the fight.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
skósmiðr þú verir
né skeptismiðr,
nema þú siálfom þér sér;
skór er skapaðr illa,
eða skapt sé rangt,
þá er þér bǫls beðit.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
A shoe-smith be you not,
nor a shaft-smith,
unless you be one for your own self;
a shoe is shaped badly,
or a shaft be crooked,
then ill is wished upon you.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: do not turn shoemaker, or shaftmaker either, for anyone but yourself: let a shoe be badly made or a shaft come out crooked, and it is you they will wish ill on.
sentences.n: Two traps in six lines. First, the Norse has no negative in skósmiðr þú verir — the né of the next line reaches back and negates both halves, a deferred negation the language allows and English does not; the literal layer supplies the 'not' because a coherent line has to have it, but nothing in the first line corresponds to it. Second, sér in line 7 is not the reflexive pronoun sér 'for himself' that the reader has met a dozen times already — it is vera, second person singular present subjunctive, 'you be'. þér beside it is the dative pronoun and siálfom agrees with it: 'unless you be [one] for your own self'. The shared glossary has been widened accordingly. And the two subjunctives of this stanza belong together: vera has two present subjunctives, one built on the s-stem (sé, sér, sé) and one on the ver-stem (vera, verir, veri), and this stanza uses one of each — verir in line 5, sér in line 7. They are the same verb wearing two faces, and nowhere else in the poem do the two stems stand so close. Then the paratactic condition: there is no ef, and the shift into the subjunctive sé in the second limb is what marks the clause as hypothetical. bǫls beðit is biðia with the genitive, in an impersonal passive with no one named as praying — 'ill is asked for you'. The counsel is about liability, not craftsmanship: make a thing for another man and his bad luck with it turns into curses aimed at you. Note what the poem does and does not say — the ill is asked for; it is not said to arrive.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
hvars þú bǫl kant,
kveðu þér bǫlvi at
ok gefat þínom fiándom frið.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
Wherever you know of harm,
speak out upon the harm as done to you
and give not peace to your foes.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: wherever you know of some harm, declare that harm done to you, and give your enemies no peace.
sentences.n: hvars is hvar es, 'where that', contracted — the same relative particle that shows up as er everywhere else in the poem. kant beside it is a plain indicative, 'you know of', not 'you come across': kunna is knowledge, not encounter, and the same hvars takes a subjunctive at 137,5, which is worth comparing. kveðu is the imperative kveð with the enclitic pronoun run onto it; the chunk is full of these (verðu 128, hafðu 132, hlæðu 134, gef 136 without one), and they are the ordinary shape of an Old Norse command to a named person. at in line 6 is postposed and governs bǫlvi: kveða at e-u is 'to pronounce upon something', so the line says that you speak out upon the harm as harm done to you — the dative þér is what makes it yours. What follows from that in practice is that you adopt the quarrel rather than let it pass, which is why the idiomatic layer can say 'declare that harm done to you' and mean a feud; the Norse names no feud. gefat is the imperative with the suffixed negative -at. Neckel's apparatus records that Gering deleted þínom in the last line and that Neckel keeps it; the apparatus gives no reason for the deletion, though the line is long with the word in. The word bǫl runs through this part — bǫls at 126, bǫl and bǫlvi here, and bǫlvi once more in the second-to-last line of 137, where runes are the remedy for it.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
illo feginn
verðu aldregi,
en lát þér at góðo getit.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
Of evil glad
become never,
but let it be spoken of you for good.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: never take pleasure in what is evil; but see to it that you are well spoken of.
sentences.n: feginn takes the dative, not the genitive — illo is dative singular neuter, 'glad of evil' — and the shared glossary, which had it as a genitive verb from an earlier chunk, is corrected here. The last line is the hard one, and it has to be taken apart before it can be translated. góðo is dative inside the prepositional phrase at góðo, so 'good' cannot be the thing gotten; getit is the neuter past participle of geta in the construction láta + participle, with no subject expressed at all; and geta e-s at góðo is a well-attested idiom meaning 'to speak of someone with approval'. Put together, the line is about reputation: let it be spoken of you for good. Neckel prints þér, the dative, and that is the harder reading, because geta normally takes the genitive of the person mentioned — which is precisely why Rask emended to þín. His apparatus entry reads '7 þér R, þín R', where the bold R is the Codex Regius and the italic R is Rask, one of the siglum collisions this poem is full of. We keep Neckel's text and take þér as a dative of reference; on either reading at góðo getit means 'mentioned with approval', so the counsel itself does not turn on the emendation. The apparatus also notes that Finnur Jónsson reads verð for the manuscript's verðu.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
upp líta
skalattu í orrosto —
gialti glíkir
verða gumna synir —
síðr þik um heilli halir.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
Up to look
you shall not in battle —
like to a man struck witless
do the sons of men become —
lest men bewitch you.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: do not look up when you are in battle — the sons of men go witless with terror — or men may lay a spell on you.
sentences.n: gialti has no recorded nominative; it exists only in the phrase verða at gialti, 'to be struck witless with terror', and the dictionaries derive it from Irish geilt, the madman who runs wild in the woods after a battle. There is an old popular association with galti 'a boar', which is why the phrase is sometimes englished as though a man went boar-mad; the lexica do not accept it, and neither layer here uses the word. glíkir is líkr with the old g- prefix and governs the dative. The middle two lines are a parenthesis: this is what happens to men, so do not do the thing that starts it. halir in the last line is the plain word for 'men' — the battle is carried by í orrosto, not by the noun, and narrowing it to fighting-men would make the spell-casters combatants, which the Norse does not say. heilli is heilla 'to bewitch' in the plural subjunctive, with the expletive um before it, and síðr … um heilli is a negative purpose clause, 'lest they bewitch you' — the same construction as at 131,10. Battle-magic that fixes a man where he stands is a real fear in the sagas. Why looking up should be what lets the spell catch is nowhere stated; the counsel assumes a connection the poem does not explain. Two apparatus notes, and the second matters: the í of í orrosto was added above the line by the Codex Regius scribe; and þik in the last line is Finn Magnusen's conjecture — the manuscript reads þitt, the neuter possessive, which will not construe with heilli. Neckel prints the emended letter in italic. The line is therefore secure in sense and not in text.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
ef þú vilt þér góða kono
kveðia at gamanrúnom
ok fá fǫgnuð af:
fǫgro skaldu heita
ok láta fast vera;
leiðiz manngi gott, ef getr.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
If you would for yourself a good woman
call into pleasure-talk
and get delight of it:
fair things shall you promise
and let them stand fast;
no one is wearied of good, if he gets it.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: if you want to bring a good woman into intimate talk and get joy of it, promise her fair things and then hold to them: nobody tires of good things, when they come to him.
sentences.n: gamanrúnar is gaman 'pleasure, delight' plus rúnar in its older sense of 'secrets, things confided' — not runic letters, not magic, and not a word for lovers' talk in particular: st. 120 used it of drawing a good man to you. Here it is a woman, and the two counsels are deliberately parallel; whatever erotic weight the stanza carries comes from the situation, not from the noun. Watch the syntax of the first two lines, because English inverts it if you let it: kveðia is an infinitive governed by vilt, kono is its accusative object, and þú is the subject of both verbs — 'if you would call a good woman to yourself into pleasure-talk'. English 'if you want a good woman to call' puts the calling on her, which is the reverse of the Norse, so the literal layer keeps 'would … call' apart from any 'want X to' shape. kveðia e-n at e-u is 'to invite someone to something'. heita governs the dative of the thing promised, hence fǫgro, neuter dative used as a noun, 'fair things'; skaldu is skalt þú. Then the sting in the tail, which is not cynical: láta fast vera is 'let it stand firm', keep the promise, because — leiðiz manngi gott — nobody ever gets tired of being treated well. Neckel's apparatus records that the Codex Regius corrected manngi from margr; the apparatus lemma spells the word mangi, while the printed text has manngi with two n's.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
varan bið ek þik vera,
ok eigi ofvaran;
ver þú við ǫl varastr
ok við annars kono
ok við þat it þriðia,
at þik þiófar ne leiki.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
Wary I bid you be,
and not over-wary;
be you most wary with ale
and with another's wife
and with that third thing,
lest thieves play you false.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: be wary, I tell you, but not too wary; be warest of all with ale, and with another man's wife, and with a third thing besides — lest thieves make a fool of you.
sentences.n: The poem's habitual second thought: it wants a quality and then immediately takes half of it back, as it did with wisdom at sts. 54–56, where the middling-wise man lives best. varr, then ofvarr, then the superlative varastr in the very next line, all from the same adjective — the stanza is built out of the degrees of one word. eigi here is the adverb 'not', not the verb eiga that the shared glossary had. leika e-n is 'to play tricks on, to make a fool of'; the shared entry, which carried only the noun leikr 'game, play' (biarnar leiki 'a bear's play', st. 86,7), now carries both, because the same form does both jobs in this poem. The last line is a negative purpose clause and not an apposition: at þik þiófar ne leiki is 'lest thieves make a fool of you', not a naming of the third thing. The third thing is left unsaid — that is the joke — and the same construction, with síðr instead of at … ne, stands at 129,9. Note too that við governs the accusative three times here (við ǫl, við annars kono, við þat it þriðia) where the same preposition takes the dative nine times at st. 137; the case is what separates 'be wary of' from 'takes up against'. The apparatus: þik in the last line is Rask's supplement — the Codex Regius has no pronoun there (f. = fehlt) — and Neckel prints the whole word in italic to mark it as editorial. He also records Resen's older reading, þik ei þiófar lyki. The counsel survives the missing word; what fails without it is metre and sense rather than grammar, since leika can stand intransitively. As the scribe left it the line has no object and is short, which is why Rask supplied one.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
at háði né hlátri
hafðu aldregi
gest né ganganda;
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
For mockery nor for laughter
hold never
a guest nor a walker;
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: never hold a guest or a man on the road up to mockery or to laughter —
sentences.n: hafa e-n at háði is a set phrase, 'to hold someone in derision', with at governing the dative of what he is held as. ganganda is the present participle of ganga used as a noun, the man who arrives on foot: a tramp, and in this poem's world also possibly a god. The semicolon is Neckel's, and it is load-bearing — the sentence does not end here. St. 133 finishes it and carries no refrain of its own, in the manuscript as in Neckel; the same thing happens at 135–136. Those refrainless continuations are the clearest sign in the text that the Loddfáfnir counsels grew: a frame that is supposed to introduce each counsel keeps failing to appear where a new counsel begins. The guest-ethic itself is the Gestaþáttr's, from sts. 2–3, come round again.

sentences.t:
opt vito ógǫrla,
þeir er sitia inni fyrir,
hvers þeir ro kyns, er koma;
erat maðr svá góðr,
at galli ne fylgi,
né svá illr, at einugi dugi.
sentences.l:
Often they know not clearly,
those who sit within doors,
of what kin they are who come;
there is no man so good
that no fault goes with him,
nor so ill that he is worth nothing.
sentences.i: — for the men sitting indoors often do not know clearly what stock the newcomers are of. There is no man so good that no fault attends him, nor any so bad that he is good for nothing.
sentences.n: The continuation of 132, printed without the refrain. hvers … kyns is a genitive of description split across the line, 'of what kin', with the noun held back to the end of the clause; ro is the old third-plural of vera. erat is er with the suffixed negative. The two subjunctives in the last three lines, fylgi and dugi, stand in consecutive clauses — 'so good that…', 'so bad that…' — and they are subjunctive because the governing clause is negated: there is no such man, so the result is hypothetical. They are not concessives, and reading them as 'although' loses the shape of the sentence. ne before fylgi is the older negative particle the poem keeps reaching for in verse. duga takes the dative, and einugi is the dative singular neuter of engi: 'avails for nothing'. The whole is one of the poem's flattest and best pieces of tolerance, and it is offered as a practical reason rather than a moral one — you cannot see what a stranger is, therefore do not price him.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
at három þul
hlæðu aldregi:
opt er gott, þat er gamlir kveða,
opt ór skǫrpom belg
skilin orð koma,
þeim er hangir með hám
ok skollir með skrám
ok váfir með vilmǫgom.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
At a hoary sage
laugh never:
often it is good, what the old ones say;
often out of a shrunken hide-bag
come sifted words,
from that one which hangs among the skins
and dangles among the dried hides
and sways among the gut-bags.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: never laugh at a grey-haired sage. What the old say is often good, and words that have been sifted often come out of a shrunken hide-bag — the one hanging there with the skins, dangling with the dried hides, swaying among the gut-bags.
sentences.n: þulr is the word from st. 111, where this whole part opened with a man speaking þular stóli á, 'on the sage's seat'. The counsel is therefore about the poem's own speaker, and the joke that follows is made at his expense and in his defence at once. The image is a storehouse: the old man's slack, wrinkled skin is a belgr, a hide stripped off whole and used as a bag, and it hangs there with the other hanging things — hám 'hides', skrám 'dried skins', vilmǫgom. The three datives chime, and the third is a genuine crux with two lexical parents, which should be named rather than smoothed. Cleasby–Vigfússon files this very line under víl-mǫgr, plural vílmegir, 'a son of toil, a bondsman', from víl 'toil, misery' — which would hang the bag among servants. Against that stands vil 'entrails' (compare vil-magi, the maw), which gives gut-bags hung up to dry and puts the third dative in the same storehouse as the first two. We follow the second on the strength of the context and record the first, because it is the reading of the dictionary that cites the line. Nobody is sure. skilin is the past participle of skilia 'to separate, to distinguish', so skilin orð are words that have been sifted — told apart from one another, clear-cut. It is a participle and not an adjective of active discernment: the words do not discern, they have been discerned, and all three layers keep it passive. þeim is dative singular masculine in apposition to belg, so the thing hanging is the bag, not the man; the identification of the two is left for the reader to make. The apparatus at this stanza is the one that shows what the scribe actually wrote for the refrain, and it is the exception to the cross-reference used everywhere else: '134, 1—4 abgek. Ráð. þér R.'

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
gest þú ne geyia
né á grind hrøkkvir,
get þú váloðom vel;
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
At a guest bark not
nor drive him to the gate,
deal well with the wretched;
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: do not bay at a guest, or chase him out to the gate; deal well with the destitute —
sentences.n: geyia is what a dog does, and using it of a man is the insult: do not bark at your visitor. The form is worth naming, because it is not the imperative it reads as in English — the imperative of geyia would be gey. This is the bare infinitive used as a prohibition, coordinated by né with the finite second-person hrøkkvir in the next line, so one command is carried by two different kinds of verb form. That asymmetry is worth noticing two stanzas after 126 carried its prohibition on a subjunctive, verir. The next half-line is emended. Neckel prints hrøkkvir with the middle letters in italic, and his apparatus gives the reason: '6 hrøkkvir H, hrǫkir R', where the italic H is the scholar Karl Hildebrand and the bold R is the Codex Regius. Bold H would have been the Hauksbók — which does transmit a piece of the Hávamál, 84,4—6, where Neckel's apparatus reads '84, 4—6 auch in FH' and cites H for readings; it is the weight of the type, not the manuscript's coverage, that tells the two H's apart, and this stanza is not in it. The manuscript's hrǫkir is not a recognised form of the verb; Hildebrand read it as a miswriting of hrøkkvir, and Neckel prints the repaired letters in italic. So 'drive him out to the gate' is a nineteenth-century repair, and the sense is inferred from the company it keeps. geta in the last line takes the dative váloðom; the verb's usual sense is 'to get', but with a dative person the natural reading is 'do well by, provide for', and some would take it as 'speak well of'. váluðr is a wretch, the man who has nothing. Neckel's semicolon runs the sentence on into 136, which again has no refrain.

sentences.t:
ramt er þat tré,
er ríða skal
ǫllom at upploki;
baug þú gef,
eða þat biðia mun
þér læs hvers á liðo.
sentences.l:
Strong is that beam
which must swing
for all at the unlocking;
a ring do you give,
or that will call down
every harm upon your limbs.
sentences.i: — the door-beam that has to swing open for everybody had better be strong. Give a ring, or that will call down every harm there is upon your limbs.
sentences.n: The continuation of 135, and one of the compressed places where the reader should be told plainly that the joins are guesswork. tré is a piece of timber, here the beam or bar of a door; ríða is used of a door turning on its hinge; and upplok is a noun, 'an opening, an unlocking', standing in the dative after at — ǫllom at upploki is 'for everyone's opening', not an infinitive of purpose. So the first three lines are 'that timber must be strong which has to swing for all comers to open'. Then a jump: baug þú gef, give a ring — the arm-ring is the standard portable wealth and the standard gift, as in the baugeiðr of st. 110 — and if you do not, þat biðia mun … læs hvers. The construction there is biðia e-m e-s, dative of the person the thing is called down upon and genitive of the thing prayed for: þér læs hvers is 'every harm upon you', an imprecation and not a request made on your behalf. þat is neuter and points most naturally back to tré, which would make the door itself the thing that prays the harm down; but þat may equally be resumptive — 'that (failure of yours) will call down…' — and the poem does not decide between them. Neckel records no variant anywhere in this stanza: the difficulty is in the sense, not in the text. What is not clear is who receives the ring, and how the open door of the first half and the gift of the second are meant to lock together.

sentences.t:
Ráðomk þér, Loddfáfnir,
en þú ráð nemir —
nióta mundo, ef þú nemr,
þér muno góð, ef þú getr —:
hvars þú ǫl drekkir,
kiós þú þér iarðar megin;
þvíat iǫrð tekr við ǫlðri,
en eldr við sóttom,
eik við abbindi,
ax við fiǫlkyngi,
*hǫll við hýrógi
— heiptom skal mána kveðia —,
beiti við bitsóttom,
en við bǫlvi rúnar,
fold skal við flóði taka.
sentences.l:
I counsel you, Loddfáfnir,
and may you take counsel —
you will have use of them, if you take them,
good they will be to you, if you get them —:
Wherever you drink ale,
choose for yourself the earth's might;
for earth takes up ale-drink,
and fire against sicknesses,
oak against constipation,
an ear of corn against witchcraft,
*the hall against household-strife
— against hatreds one shall call on the moon —,
beiti against the biting sicknesses,
and against bane, runes,
the land shall take up the flood.
sentences.i: I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, and may you take the counsel — you will profit if you learn them, they will do you good if you get them —: wherever you drink ale, choose the earth's strength for yourself; for earth takes up drunkenness, and fire sickness, oak constipation, an ear of grain witchcraft, *the hall strife at home (that half-line is broken in the text) — against hatreds you must call upon the moon — beiti the biting sicknesses, and runes take up bane; and it is the land that must take up the flood.
sentences.n: The Loddfáfnir counsels end in a list of remedies, one ill to each cure, and the syntax is a single frame repeated with the verb left out after its first appearance: the cure stands in the nominative, við governs the dative of the thing cured, and taka við is understood down the whole catalogue until fold skal við flóði taka spells it out again at the end. taka við e-u is 'to receive, to take charge of' — that is all the dictionaries give it. The remedial force, 'absorbs, counteracts', is inferred from what the catalogue is doing and is not a recorded sense of the phrase; and English 'take against' would be a false friend, since in English it means to conceive a dislike for something. Both layers therefore say 'takes up'. Note also that við takes the dative nine times here where it took the accusative three times at st. 131: the case is doing the work. iǫrð at the head and fold at the foot are the same thing said with two words, and the list is enclosed between them — which is why both are 'earth' and 'land' in the literal layer and neither is 'field'. Some of the pairs are transparent (fire against sickness, runes against bǫl, the word that has been running through this part since st. 126); some are folk medicine we can only report (earth swallowing drunkenness; an ear of grain against sorcery; abbindi is constipation, and oak is the cure); and two are not soluble. — The first is line 11, which Neckel marks with an asterisk as corrupt, and both layers carry the mark. As printed it says 'hall against hýrógi', and hýróg looks like hý- 'household' (as in hýbýli) plus róg 'strife' — the hall against strife at home. But Vigfússon's dictionary proposed reading við haulvi hýrógr, or hýrógr við haul, and glossed it in English as 'spurred rye — ergot of rye — against hernia'; Mogk prints við haulvi hýrogr, Sijmons hýrogi. That would put the line in the same register as abbindi. We translate what Neckel prints, with his asterisk, and say plainly that the half-line is broken. — The second is beiti. The shared glossary carries it from st. 90 as a poetic word for a ship, which is the sense the medieval name-lists give and which cannot possibly be right here; against bitsóttir the word must be a plant or a remedy, and the dictionaries do not agree what. The entry has been widened to say so rather than to guess. — heiptom is a bare dative in a list of við-datives, so it is most likely the ill and not the instrument: against hatreds, invoke the moon. kveðia here takes a plain accusative, mána, and means 'to call upon, to invoke' — not the kveðia e-n at e-u of st. 130; and kiósa at line 6 is 'to choose, to pick out', which is why the idiomatic layer says 'choose' there and keeps 'call upon' for kveðia. Two small apparatus notes: the Codex Regius writes drekkir with the abbreviation for -ir, and most editors resolve it as drekkr — but the choice is a choice of mood, since drekkr is the second-person indicative of this strong verb and drekkir the subjunctive, so Neckel's printed text has a subjunctive after hvars where 127,5 had the indicative kant; and øx 'axe' for ax 'ear of corn' is a conjecture recorded from Wimmer and Cederschiöld — both scholars, not manuscripts. — With this stanza the part ends. Müllenhoff moved st. 164, the poem's last, to follow here; the paper manuscripts head what comes next Rúnatals þáttr Óðins; and the Codex Regius itself marks the break, as Neckel notes, by writing the opening letter of 138,1 outsized — Neckel calls it a U, which is the manuscript's letterform for the V of Veit ek, at ek hekk.
